source_refs.note: Chapter 4 exercise (PDF 89-92, printed 86-89), solved: MCQ keys worked out from the chapter (the book prints none), model answers for the short, constructed response and comprehensive questions, and step-by-step numerical solutions checked against the printed answers.

blocks.prompt: 4.1 A 1 kg mass has potential energy of 1 joule relative to the ground when it is at a height of:
blocks.explanation: P.E. = mgh, so h = P.E./(mg) = 1 J ÷ (1 kg × 9.8 m s⁻²) = 0.102 m.

blocks.prompt: 4.2 An iron sphere whose mass is 30 kg has the same diameter as an aluminium sphere whose mass is 10.5 kg. The spheres are simultaneously dropped from a cliff. When they are 10 m from the ground, they have identical:
blocks.explanation: Both fall freely with the same acceleration g = 9.8 m s⁻² (and so have the same speed at each height). Their momentum mv, P.E. mgh and K.E. ½mv² all depend on mass, so they are different.

blocks.prompt: 4.3 A body at rest may have:
blocks.explanation: At rest v = 0, so speed, velocity and momentum are zero, but the body can have potential energy due to its position (e.g. mgh) or its compressed state.

blocks.prompt: 4.4 The height above the ground of a child on a swing varies from 0.5 m of his lowest point to 1.5 m at his highest point. The maximum speed of the child is approximately:
blocks.explanation: Loss in P.E. = gain in K.E.: mgh = ½mv², h = 1.5 − 0.5 = 1.0 m. v = √(2gh) = √(2 × 9.8 × 1.0) = 4.4 m s⁻¹ (mass cancels).

blocks.prompt: 4.5 When a ball is thrown vertically upward and then falls back to the ground, which force can be considered conservative in this scenario?
blocks.explanation: The work done by gravity is independent of the path and is zero for the round trip, so gravity is conservative. Air resistance and friction are non-conservative (4.3).

blocks.prompt: 4.6 According to work-energy principle in linear motion, the work done on body is equal to:
blocks.explanation: Work-energy theorem: the work done on a body by the net force equals the change in its kinetic energy, W = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i² (4.7).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The fourth option is printed with the label (b) again: "(b) sum of K.E. and P.E.". It is option (d).

blocks.prompt: 4.7 Power of a lamp is 6 W. How much energy does a lamp give out in 2 min?
4.8 A dry battery can deliver 3000 J of energy to a 2 W small electric motor before the battery is exhausted. For how many minutes does the battery run?
4.9 The kinetic energy acquired by a mass m after travelling a fixed distance from rest under the action of a constant force is directly proportional to:
blocks.explanation: By the work-energy theorem, K.E. gained = work done = Fd. For a fixed force F and distance d it is the same for any mass, so it is independent of m.

blocks.prompt: 4.10 A body moves a distance of 10 m along a straight line under the action of 5 N force. If the work done is 25 J, the angle which the force makes with the direction of motion of the body is:
blocks.explanation: W = Fd cos θ: 25 = 5 × 10 × cos θ, cos θ = 0.5, θ = 60°.

blocks.prompt: 4.1 Why is electrical power required at all when the elevator is descending? Why should be there be a limit on the number of passengers in this case?
blocks.explanation:
Power is needed to control the descent: the motor (with brakes) works against gravity so that the lift comes down at a safe, steady speed and stops at each floor; it also raises the counterweight and overcomes friction.
The larger the load, the larger the force needed to hold and stop it; the cable and motor can bear only a limited force, so the number of passengers must be limited.

blocks.prompt: 4.2. A body is being raised to a height H from surface of Earth. What is the sign of work done by both? justify.
blocks.explanation:
Work done by the lifting force is positive, because the force and displacement are both upward (θ = 0°): W = +mgH.
Work done by gravity is negative, because mg is downward and the displacement is upward (θ = 180°): W = −mgH.

blocks.prompt: 4.3 A body falls towards the Earth in air. Will its total mechanical energy be conserved during fall? Justify.
blocks.explanation:
No. Air resistance (a non-conservative force) acts against the motion, and part of the P.E. is used in doing work against it (changed into heat).
Loss in P.E. = gain in K.E. + work done against friction (mgh = ½mv² + fh), so the total mechanical energy decreases.

blocks.prompt: 4.4 Calculate power of a crane in kilowatt which lifts a mass of 1000 kg to a height of 100 m in 20 second.

4.5 A trolley of mass 1500 kg carrying sand bags of 500 kg is moving uniformly with a speed of 40 km h⁻¹ on a frictionless track. After some time, sand starts leaking out of whole sand bags on the road at a rate of 0.05 kg s⁻¹. What is the speed of the trolley after entire sand bags are empty?
blocks.explanation:
The speed stays 40 km h⁻¹.
The sand leaks out with the same forward velocity as the trolley, so it carries away its own momentum and exerts no horizontal force on the trolley; on the frictionless track no external force acts, so the trolley's velocity does not change.

blocks.prompt: 4.6 When will you say that a force is conservative? Also give an example.
blocks.explanation:
A force is conservative if the work done by it in moving a body between two points is independent of the path followed, or the work done along a closed path is zero.
Example: gravitational force (also electrostatic and elastic spring force).

blocks.prompt: 4.7 Give absolute and gravitational units of work on M.K.S & C.G.S systems.
blocks.explanation:
M.K.S: absolute unit = joule (1 J = 1 N × 1 m); gravitational unit = kilogram-weight metre (1 kg-wt m = 9.8 J).
C.G.S: absolute unit = erg (1 erg = 1 dyne × 1 cm = 10⁻⁷ J); gravitational unit = gram-weight centimetre (1 g-wt cm = 980 erg).

blocks.prompt: 4.8 A body dropped from a height of H reaches the ground with a speed of 1.2√(gH). Calculate work done by air friction.
blocks.explanation:
K.E. at the ground = ½m(1.2√(gH))² = ½m × 1.44gH = 0.72 mgH
Loss in P.E. = mgH
Work done by air friction = K.E. − mgH = 0.72 mgH − mgH = −0.28 mgH
(i.e. 0.28 mgH of energy is used against air friction).

blocks.prompt:
4.9 A bicycle has a K.E. of 150 J. What K.E. would the bicycle have if it had?
(i) Same mass but has speed double?
(ii) Three times mass and was moving with one half of the speed?
4.10 What will be the effect on K.E. of the body having mass m, moving with velocity v when its momentum becomes double? Justify.
blocks.explanation:
K.E. becomes four times.
K.E. = ½mv² = p²/2m. If p becomes 2p (mass same), K.E. = (2p)²/2m = 4 × p²/2m.

blocks.prompt: 4.11 Does the international space-station have gravitation P.E. or/and Kinetic energy? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
It has both.
It moves in its orbit with a large speed (about 7.7 km s⁻¹), so it has K.E. = ½mv².
It is in the Earth's gravitational field at distance r from the centre, so it has gravitational P.E. U = −GMm/r (negative, but greater than at the Earth's surface).

blocks.prompt: 4.1 When will you say that a force is conservative? Give two conditions.
blocks.explanation:
A force is called conservative if:
1. The work done by it in moving a body from one point to another is independent of the path followed (it depends only on the initial and final positions). E.g. gravity does work −mgh from A to B along any path.
2. The work done by it along a closed path is zero (e.g. along ACBA, W = −mgh + mgh = 0).
Examples: gravitational force, electrostatic force and elastic spring force. Friction and air resistance are non-conservative.

blocks.prompt: 4.2 A light and heavy body have same linear momentum, which one has greater K.E.?
blocks.explanation:
The lighter body has greater K.E.
K.E. = ½mv² = p²/2m.
For the same momentum p, K.E. ∝ 1/m, so the body with smaller mass has larger K.E. (it must move with a much larger speed to have the same momentum).

blocks.prompt: 4.3 A motorcycle is running with constant speed on a horizontal track. Is any work being done on the motorcycle, if no net force is acting on it?
blocks.explanation:
No net work is done on it.
By the work-energy theorem, net work = change in K.E. The speed is constant, so ΔK.E. = 0 and the net work is zero (W = F_net d = 0 as F_net = 0).
However, the engine's driving force does positive work and friction/air resistance do an equal negative work; the two cancel. On a horizontal track gravity and the normal force do no work (they are perpendicular to the motion).

blocks.prompt: 4.4 A force acts on a ball moving with 14 m s⁻¹ speed and brings its speed to 6 m s⁻¹. Has the force done positive or negative work? Explain your answer.
blocks.explanation:
The force has done negative work.
By the work-energy theorem, W = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i² = ½m(6² − 14²) = ½m(36 − 196) = −80m J (m in kg).
The K.E. of the ball decreases, so W is negative; the force acts opposite to the motion (θ > 90°).

blocks.prompt: 4.5 A slow moving truck can have more kinetic energy than a fast moving car. How is this possible?
blocks.explanation:
K.E. = ½mv² depends on mass as well as speed.
A truck has a very large mass compared with a car. Even with a smaller speed, its large mass can make ½mv² greater.
Example: truck m = 10 000 kg, v = 10 m s⁻¹: K.E. = 5 × 10⁵ J; car m = 1000 kg, v = 20 m s⁻¹: K.E. = 2 × 10⁵ J. The slow truck has more K.E.

blocks.prompt: 4.6 Why work done against friction is non-conservative in nature? Explain briefly.
blocks.explanation:
Kinetic friction always acts opposite to the motion, so it does negative work equal to f × (length of the path).
1. The work therefore depends on the path: a longer path between the same two points needs more work.
2. On a closed path (returning to the start) the work done against friction is not zero; it adds up on both ways.
3. This energy is changed into heat and is not recovered as mechanical energy.
Hence friction is a non-conservative force.

blocks.prompt: 4.7 Does wind contain kinetic energy? Explain.
blocks.explanation:
Yes. Wind is moving air; air has mass and the wind has velocity, so it has K.E. = ½mv².
This energy can do work: wind turns windmills and wind turbines (to produce electricity), moves sailing boats, and strong winds can uproot trees and damage buildings.

blocks.prompt: 4.1 Define K.E. Derive an expression for the same.
blocks.explanation:
Kinetic energy: the energy possessed by a body due to its motion is called kinetic energy.

Derivation:
A car of mass m moves with speed v. When its engine is switched off, it still covers a distance d before stopping; while moving it does work against the force of friction f. So its K.E. = work done against friction = fd.
The friction produces a negative acceleration: f = −ma, or a = −f/m.
Using the third equation of motion: 2aS = v_f² − v_i²
with v_i = v, v_f = 0, S = d, a = −f/m:
2 × (−f/m) × d = 0 − v²
fd = ½mv²
As fd equals the kinetic energy of the body:
K.E. = ½mv²   (Eq. 4.9)
Its unit is the same as that of work, joule (J). K.E. is a scalar quantity.

blocks.prompt:
4.2 How work is done by a:
(i) constant force (ii) variable force?
blocks.explanation:
(i) Work done by a constant force:
When a constant force F displaces a body through d in its own direction: W = Fd.
If F makes an angle θ with the displacement, only the component F cos θ along d does work:
W = (F cos θ) d = Fd cos θ, or W = F⃗ · d⃗ (a scalar). Unit: joule (1 J = 1 N m).
θ < 90°: positive work; θ = 90°: no work; θ > 90°: negative work.
On a force-displacement graph the constant force is a horizontal line and the work is the area of the rectangle under it (F × d).

(ii) Work done by a variable force:
The path from P to Q is divided into n small displacements Δd₁, Δd₂, …, Δdₙ, so small that the force F₁, F₂, …, Fₙ is nearly constant in each.
ΔW₁ = F₁ cos θ₁ Δd₁, ΔW₂ = F₂ cos θ₂ Δd₂, …
W_total = Σ Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ   (Eq. 4.4)
On a graph of F cos θ versus d, each term is the area of a thin rectangle. Taking Δd → 0:
W_total = lim(Δd→0) Σ Fᵢ cos θᵢ Δdᵢ   (Eq. 4.5)
So the work done by a variable force between P and Q equals the area under the F cos θ versus d curve between P and Q. Example: work against the gravity on a rocket moving away from the Earth, or in stretching a spring.

blocks.prompt: 4.3 Define conservative field. Show that gravitational field is conservative in nature.
blocks.explanation:
Conservative field: a field in which the work done in moving a body from one point to another is independent of the path followed, or the work done along a closed path is zero. (The space around the Earth in which its gravitational force acts is the gravitational field.)

Proof for the gravitational field:
A body of mass m is moved with constant speed from A to B, where B is a height h above A. The gravitational force is its weight mg, acting downward.
Path 1 (ADB): along AD (horizontal) work = 0, since mg ⊥ displacement; along DB (upward) work = −mgh.
W_ADB = 0 + (−mgh) = −mgh
Path 2 (ACB): along AC (upward) work = −mgh; along CB (horizontal) work = 0.
W_ACB = −mgh + 0 = −mgh
Path 3 (any curved path AB): break it into small horizontal and vertical steps. No work along horizontal steps; along vertical steps:
W_AB = −mg(Δy₁ + Δy₂ + … + Δyₙ) = −mgh, since Δy₁ + Δy₂ + … + Δyₙ = h.
The work done is −mgh along every path, so it is independent of the path.
Also along a closed path, e.g. ACBA: W = −mgh (A to B) + mgh (B back to A) = 0.
Hence the gravitational field is a conservative field.

blocks.prompt: 4.4 What is meant by absolute P.E.? Derive an expression for absolute P.E.
blocks.explanation:
Absolute potential energy: the absolute gravitational P.E. of a body at a position is the work done by the gravitational force in displacing the body from that position to infinity, where the force of gravity becomes zero.

Derivation:
mgh is valid only near the Earth's surface; over a large distance the force F = GMm/r² changes. So the distance from point 1 (r₁ from the Earth's centre) to point N is divided into small steps of length Δr, in each of which the force is nearly constant.
For the first step (r₁ to r₂), the mid-distance r = (r₁ + r₂)/2 = r₁ + Δr/2
r² = r₁² + r₁Δr + (Δr/2)² ≈ r₁² + r₁Δr (neglecting (Δr)²)
= r₁² + r₁(r₂ − r₁) = r₁r₂
Force in this step: F = GMm/(r₁r₂)
Work done by gravity (force opposite to displacement, θ = 180°):
W₁→₂ = F Δr cos 180° = −GMm (r₂ − r₁)/(r₁r₂) = −GMm (1/r₁ − 1/r₂)
Similarly: W₂→₃ = −GMm (1/r₂ − 1/r₃), …, W_(N−1)→N = −GMm (1/r_(N−1) − 1/r_N)
Total work: W_total = −GMm [(1/r₁ − 1/r₂) + (1/r₂ − 1/r₃) + … + (1/r_(N−1) − 1/r_N)]
W_total = −GMm (1/r₁ − 1/r_N)
If point N is at infinity, r_N = ∞ and 1/r_N = 0:
W_total = −GMm/r₁
This work is the absolute P.E.: U = −GMm/r
On the Earth's surface (r = R): U_g = −GMm/R   (Eq. 4.13)
The negative sign shows that the gravitational field is attractive; GMm/R is the energy needed to take the body out of the Earth's gravitational field. As r increases, U becomes less negative, i.e. the P.E. increases.

blocks.prompt: 4.5 State and explain work-energy theorem in a resistive medium.
blocks.explanation:
Work-energy theorem: the change in kinetic energy of an object is equal to the work done on it by the net force.
Proof: a force F acts on a body of mass m moving with v_i through a distance d and increases its velocity to v_f.
2ad = v_f² − v_i², so a = (v_f² − v_i²)/2d; and a = F/m.
F/m = (v_f² − v_i²)/2d
Fd = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²   (Eq. 4.18)
W = (K.E.)_f − (K.E.)_i

In a resistive medium (with friction or air resistance f):
Part of the work or energy is used against the resistive force, so only the rest changes the K.E.
• Applied force F with friction f over distance d: (F − f)d = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i², i.e. work done by F = gain in K.E. + work done against friction (fd).
• A body of mass m falling from height h through air: part of the P.E. is used against friction (fh), the remaining P.E. becomes K.E.:
mgh − fh = ½mv², or mgh = ½mv² + fh   (Eq. 4.21)
Loss in P.E. = Gain in K.E. + Work done against friction
Conversely, for a body moving up: Loss of K.E. = Gain in P.E. + Work done against friction.
The work done against friction is changed into heat, so the mechanical energy is not conserved in a resistive medium.

blocks.prompt: 4.6 Define escape velocity. Show that an expression for escape velocity can be expressed as √(2Rg), where R and g denote radius of the Earth and acceleration due to gravity, respectively. Also find its numerical value.
blocks.explanation:
Escape velocity: the initial velocity of an object with which it goes out of the Earth's gravitational field is known as escape velocity.

Derivation:
The body escapes if its initial K.E. carries it to an infinite distance.
Initial K.E. = ½mv_esc²
Work needed to lift the body from the surface (U = −GMm/R) to infinity (U = 0):
Increase in P.E. = 0 − (−GMm/R) = GMm/R
The body escapes when initial K.E. = increase in P.E.:
½mv_esc² = GMm/R
v_esc = √(2GM/R)   (Eq. 4.14)
As g = GM/R², GM/R = gR:
v_esc = √(2gR)   (Eq. 4.15)

Numerical value (g = 9.8 m s⁻², R = 6.4 × 10⁶ m):
v_esc = √(2 × 9.8 m s⁻² × 6.4 × 10⁶ m)
= √(1.254 × 10⁸ m² s⁻²)
= 1.12 × 10⁴ m s⁻¹ ≈ 11.2 km s⁻¹ (about 11 km s⁻¹)
It does not depend on the mass of the body.

blocks.prompt: 4.1 A machine gun fires 6 bullets per minute with a velocity of 700 m s⁻¹. If each bullet has a mass of 40 g, then find power developed by the gun? (Ans: 9800 watt)
blocks.explanation:
Given: n = 6 bullets per minute; t = 1 min = 60 s; v = 700 m s⁻¹; m = 40 g = 0.04 kg
Required: power P = ?
K.E. of one bullet = ½mv² = ½ × 0.04 kg × (700 m s⁻¹)² = 9800 J
Energy given in one minute = 6 × 9800 J = 58 800 J
P = W/t = 58 800 J ÷ 60 s
P = 980 W

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints (Ans: 9800 watt). 9800 J is the kinetic energy of one bullet, not the power. Six bullets per minute give 6 × 9800 J = 58 800 J in 60 s, so P = 980 W. (9800 W would need 60 bullets per minute.)

blocks.prompt: 4.2 A family uses 10 kW of power. Direct solar energy is incident on horizontal surface at an average rate of 300 per square metre. If 75% of this energy can be converted into useful electrical energy, how large area is needed to supply 10 kW? (Ans: 44.44 m²)
blocks.explanation:
Given: required power P = 10 kW = 10 000 W; solar power = 300 W m⁻²; efficiency = 75%
Required: area A = ?
Useful power per square metre = 75% of 300 W m⁻² = 0.75 × 300 = 225 W m⁻²
A = required power ÷ useful power per m²
A = 10 000 W ÷ 225 W m⁻²
A = 44.44 m²

blocks.prompt: 4.3 If mass of the Earth is 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg and mass of Sun is 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg. The sun is 160 million km away from the Earth. Find the value of gravitational P.E. of the Earth. (Ans: ≈ −4.97 × 10³³ J)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m (Earth) = 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg; M (Sun) = 1.99 × 10³⁰ kg
r = 160 million km = 160 × 10⁶ × 10³ m = 1.6 × 10¹¹ m; G = 6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ N m² kg⁻²
Required: gravitational P.E. U = ?
U = −GMm/r
U = −(6.67 × 10⁻¹¹ × 1.99 × 10³⁰ × 6.0 × 10²⁴) ÷ 1.6 × 10¹¹ J
U = −(79.6 × 10⁴³) ÷ (1.6 × 10¹¹) J
U ≈ −4.97 × 10³³ J

blocks.prompt: 4.4 Water in a bucket tied with rope is whirled around in a vertical circle radius 0.5 m. Calculate minimum velocity at the lowest point so that water does not spill from it. (Ans: 4.94 m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: r = 0.5 m; g = 9.8 m s⁻²
Required: minimum velocity at the lowest point v_b = ?
At the top, water does not spill if its weight just provides the centripetal force:
mg = mv_t²/r, so v_t² = gr
From the lowest point to the top the water rises 2r; by conservation of energy:
½mv_b² = ½mv_t² + mg(2r)
v_b² = gr + 4gr = 5gr
v_b = √(5gr) = √(5 × 9.8 m s⁻² × 0.5 m)
v_b = √(24.5 m² s⁻²)
v_b = 4.95 m s⁻¹ ≈ 4.94 m s⁻¹ (as printed)

blocks.prompt:
4.5 A 75 watt fan is used for 8 hours daily for 30 days. Find:
(i) energy consumed in electrical units
(ii) electricity bill of fan if one unit cost is Rs. 22.5? (Ans: (i) 18 units (ii) Rs. 405)
blocks.explanation:
Given: P = 75 W = 0.075 kW; t = 8 h × 30 = 240 h; cost = Rs. 22.5 per unit
(i) Energy = Pt = 0.075 kW × 240 h = 18 kW h
1 unit = 1 kW h, so energy = 18 units
(ii) Bill = 18 units × Rs. 22.5
Bill = Rs. 405

blocks.prompt:
4.6 If an object of mass 2 kg is thrown up from ground reaches a height of 5 m and falls back to the Earth (neglecting air resistance), calculate:
(i) work done by gravity when object reaches at 5 m height.
(ii) work done by gravity when the object comes back to the Earth.
(iii) total work done by gravity in upward and downward motion. Also mention physical significance of the result.
[Ans: (i) −98 J (ii) +98 J (iii) 0 J significant gravity does not transfer any energy to object]
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 2 kg; h = 5 m; g = 9.8 m s⁻²
(i) Going up: mg is downward, displacement upward (θ = 180°)
W₁ = mgh cos 180° = −2 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 5 m = −98 J
(ii) Coming down: mg and displacement both downward (θ = 0°)
W₂ = mgh cos 0° = +98 J
(iii) Total work = W₁ + W₂ = −98 J + 98 J = 0 J
Significance: over the closed path (up and back) the work done by gravity is zero, so gravity is a conservative force. Gravity gives no net energy to the object: the K.E. it took away going up is returned coming down, and the object returns with the same speed.

blocks.prompt:
4.7 An electrical motor of one horse power is used to run a water pump. Water pump takes 15 minutes to fill a tank of 400 litres at a height of 10 m. Find:
(a) actual work done by electric motor to full the tank
(b) percentage efficiency of motor. Assume that mass of 1 litre of water = 1 kg). [Ans: (a) 671400 J (b) 11.6 %]
blocks.explanation:
Given: P = 1 hp = 746 W; t = 15 min = 900 s; m = 400 litres = 400 kg; h = 10 m
(a) Actual work done by the motor (input energy):
W_in = Pt = 746 W × 900 s
W_in = 671 400 J
(b) Useful work (raising the water):
W_out = mgh = 400 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 10 m = 39 200 J
Efficiency = (W_out ÷ W_in) × 100%
= (39 200 J ÷ 671 400 J) × 100%
= 5.84 %

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints 11.6 % for part (b). With the printed data the useful work is mgh = 400 × 9.8 × 10 = 39 200 J and the input is 671 400 J, so the efficiency is 5.84 %. (11.6 % is twice this; it would need 800 litres, or a height of 20 m.) Part (a), 671 400 J, is correct.

blocks.prompt: 4.8 A passenger just arrived at the airport and dragging his suitcase to luggage check in desk. He pulls strap with a force of 200 N at an angle of 45° to the floor to displace it 50 m to the desk. Determine the value of work done by him on the suitcase. (Ans: 7 kJ)
blocks.explanation:
Given: F = 200 N; θ = 45°; d = 50 m
Required: work W = ?
W = Fd cos θ
W = 200 N × 50 m × cos 45°
W = 10 000 × 0.707 J
W = 7071 J ≈ 7 kJ

blocks.prompt: 4.9 A body of mass 0.5 kg travels in a straight line with velocity v = ay^(3/2), where a = 5 m s⁻². Find the work done by the net force when it travels during the displacement from y = 0 to 5 m. (Ans: 781.25 J)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 0.5 kg; v = ay^(3/2) with a = 5 (SI units); y from 0 to 5 m
Required: work done by the net force W = ?
At y = 0: v_i = 5 × 0 = 0
At y = 5 m: v_f = 5 × 5^(3/2) = 5 × 11.18 = 55.9 m s⁻¹, so v_f² = 25 × 5³ = 3125 m² s⁻²
By the work-energy theorem: W = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i²
W = ½ × 0.5 kg × 3125 m² s⁻² − 0
W = 781.25 J

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The power of y is printed faintly; it is read as 3/2, which gives the printed answer 781.25 J. The unit printed for a (m s⁻²) does not fit v = ay^(3/2): for v in m s⁻¹ and y in m, a must be in m^(−1/2) s⁻¹. The working uses a = 5 in SI units.

blocks.prompt: 4.10 A 200 g apple is lifted to 10 m and then dropped. What is its velocity when it hits the ground? Assume that 75% of work done in lifting the apple is transferred to K.E. by the time it hits the ground. (Ans: 12.1 m s⁻¹)
blocks.explanation:
Given: m = 200 g = 0.2 kg; h = 10 m; 75% of the work becomes K.E.
Required: v = ?
Work done in lifting = mgh = 0.2 kg × 9.8 m s⁻² × 10 m = 19.6 J
K.E. at the ground = 75% of 19.6 J = 0.75 × 19.6 = 14.7 J
½mv² = 14.7 J
v² = 2 × 14.7 J ÷ 0.2 kg = 147 m² s⁻²
v = 12.1 m s⁻¹
